metadata.document: Environmental Defence Society submission on the Natural and Built Environment Bill and Spatial Planning Bill

cleaned_body_text: Environmental Defence Society submission on the Natural and Built Environment Bill and Spatial Planning Bill. SUBMITTER DETAILS: FULL NAME: Environmental Defence Society Incorporated. ADDRESS FOR SERVICE: PO Box 91736, Victoria Street West, Auckland 1142. CONTACT: Greg Severinsen, Gary Taylor. EMAIL: greg@eds.org.nz; gary@eds.org.nz. 1. Introduction. The Environmental Defence Society (EDS) thanks the Environment Select Committee for the opportunity to make a submission on the Natural and Built Environment Bill (NBEB) and Spatial Planning Bill (SPB). EDS is a not-for-profit organisation dedicated to achieving good environmental outcomes for all New Zealanders. It is active in capacities as a litigator, a policy think tank, and a conference organiser. Most of our comments relate to the NBEB, being the more complex regulatory statute and in our view the one in need of most attention. 2. Elements that we support. EDS supports the need for reform, and we see a clear case for change. The Resource Management Act 1991 (RMA) is no longer fit for purpose from an environmental standpoint. The Bills in their current form need substantive improvements. EDS's overriding concern is that the Bills need to be fit for purpose in ensuring good outcomes for the natural environment. Ultimately, a thriving natural environment benefits people as well. The NBEB, in particular, will be the country's core environmental legislation. Despite the need for significant amendment, the passage of the Bills through the House should not be delayed. 3. High-level issues. We also wish to flag some conceptual or cross-cutting elements that are problematic and require attention at the big picture level: the NBEB contains multiple mechanisms by which environmental protections can be undermined; there is no clear hierarchy between multiple outcomes; there are too many undefined, conflicting and overlapping concepts; there is too much scope for Ministerial discretion; drafting is unclear and inconsistent; and there are too few mechanisms by which decision-makers can be held accountable. 4. The overall length and structure of the legislation. The NBEB is very long, comprising over 800 pages and 861 sections as well as detailed schedules. The NBEB is more complex than necessary due to structural choices and an unnecessarily complicated drafting style. Consenting process takes up a large part of the Bill and much of this content would be better contained within schedules. Core provisions for environmental limits/targets, allocation, and protected areas should be found in more visible and cross-cutting places. 5. More detailed comments on the NBEB. Part 1 of the NBEB outlines its purpose and core principles. Part 2 outlines duties and restrictions. Part 3 outlines the National Planning Framework. Part 4 outlines Natural and Built Environment Plans. Part 5 outlines the consenting framework. We see the framework for mandatory environmental limits and associated targets as being at the core of the Bill, but the conceptualisation in the Bill is flawed and needs to be revisited. The effects management framework outlines a means of managing adverse effects, but has weaknesses and complex interactions with the protection of places of national importance like significant biodiversity areas. Comments on the Spatial Planning Bill: we see the main benefit of the SPB as being to provide better integration between various aspects of the system. Concluding comments: while reform is necessary, and we think the Bills represent an improvement on many aspects of the RMA, a number of fixes are required, most notably in the NBEB's framework for setting limits, targets and outcomes.
